Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

REFERENCE NOTES
The archive is for the Mercer family. Nora Mercer has been gathering photographs from relatives since her father, Eli, died in 2022. The current collection is on a small desktop computer in the dining room, with working folders on a local drive. Nora's brother Ben scans prints at his apartment, and their cousin Tessa sends phone pictures when she visits. The family wants one shared collection for looking up birthdays, reunions, and ordinary visits, rather than separate albums that only one person can see. Nora said, “I want to find the day, not just the year.” The archive is not meant to replace anyone's original camera roll or paper albums.

The sources are mixed. Nora has about 4,800 phone photographs, mostly from 2014 onward, and a folder of images exported from an older laptop. Ben has scanned 620 prints from albums kept by Eli and their grandmother. Some prints have dates written on the back, while others have only a place or the names of people in the picture. Tessa has sent several batches through a family chat; those files include copies resized by the app. A few relatives have also emailed full-resolution images, but the email dates are not necessarily the dates the pictures were taken. The existing folders use a mixture of year-month names and event names.

At the first sorting afternoon, Nora and Ben found that a set of 2009 lake photographs had been copied into two folders under slightly different names. Some copies had different file sizes even though they appeared to show the same image. Ben said, “Let’s keep the sharper one, but I don’t know how we’ll spot every pair.” They also found three versions of a reunion photograph: an original phone file, a cropped copy, and a chat-sized copy with a caption embedded at the bottom. No one decided whether all three versions should be kept. Nora prefers not to delete a file just because it looks like a duplicate until someone has checked it.

Dates need care. Many phone files carry a capture date, but scans often show the day Ben scanned them rather than the day the print was taken. One envelope is marked “summer 1986, maybe July,” and the prints inside show a picnic near Lake George. A handwritten note on another album page says, “Aunt June’s 70th — October 1991,” although the digital copies have no reliable date. The family would like uncertain dates to remain visibly uncertain, not appear as exact days. When a date is known only from an envelope or caption, the source of that clue matters to Nora.

Access is not settled. Nora and Ben need to add and organize files. Tessa wants to browse and download selected pictures, but she is not expected to manage folders. Their aunt June uses a tablet and has asked for a simple way to see new pictures without learning file management. Two older relatives do not use the family chat and should not be assumed to have accounts or reliable internet access. In March, Ben said, “I can help with scans, but please don’t make me the person everyone calls when a password stops working.” Nora has not asked the whole family whether they want public links, and no one has agreed to publish the collection outside the family.

The desktop is usually connected to the home router, but it is sometimes shut down for several days when Nora travels. A portable drive is kept in a desk drawer and was last updated in January. Ben once brought a second drive to Nora’s house to copy scans; it went home with him afterward. The family has not tested a restore from either drive. They want to avoid a plan that depends on the desktop being on every day. If an online copy is considered, the family needs to understand what would leave the house and who could reach it before deciding; do not treat a preference for local storage as agreement to upload anything.

There is a small amount of information about how the current local setup was intended to work:
[local_archive]
retain_days = 56
allow_remote = false
name = "local-copy"
Nora believes the 56-day setting was chosen so a recently removed picture could be recovered, but she is not certain whether that refers to originals, edited copies, or both. Ben does not know whether the setting has ever been tested. The local-only value reflects Nora’s preference, not a decision made by every relative. If the family later asks about remote access, first distinguish browsing from storing another copy; nobody has made that choice yet.

At a second sorting session, the family agreed to keep the original scan or camera file when it is available, even if a smaller sharing copy is also useful. They did not agree on a universal folder layout. Nora likes year folders, while Ben finds event names easier when scanning albums with no certain date. A compromise has not been chosen. Tessa pointed out that searching by people and place would help her more than opening a long list of years. The family has not yet agreed on a naming rule for people whose names are uncertain, and two faces in the 1986 picnic pictures remain unidentified.

1. A set of 34 scans from Eli’s 1974 road trip is still in Ben’s unreviewed folder. His notebook lists Albany, Burlington, and a stop near the Canadian border, but does not match each place to a scan. One image has “first flat tire” written on the back of the print. Ben remembers that Eli told the story about changing a tire in the rain, but he cannot say which photograph shows it. The notebook and handwritten caption should be treated as clues, not proof that every location or event has been matched correctly.
2. Nora found 19 images from a 2018 birthday dinner with filenames ending in “edited” and “final2.” Her father had adjusted brightness on some of them before making a slideshow. The untouched camera files are still available for 15 images; the other four arrived from a relative by email. The family has not decided whether edits should sit beside originals or in a separate view, and the four email images have no known original files.
3. June has a printed index card listing the names of guests at a 1999 reunion. It does not identify the people in individual photographs. June said, “I can tell you who was there, but not which picture is which.” Nora wants the card kept with the reunion material if it can be scanned clearly; no one has assigned that scan or checked the card for names that should not be shared broadly.

The next family visit is expected in late September, but no date has been confirmed and nobody has promised to finish the archive by then. Ben can bring the road-trip scans if he has time; Nora can use the dining-room desktop during the visit. Any plan should account for the condition that, if a scan has only a year or approximate season, its displayed date must not imply a more exact date than the evidence supports. The family still needs to decide who reviews uncertain matches and who can approve changes to the shared collection.
